# Empirical Status

The theory's best feature is that it is squeezed from two sides at once and cannot escape by tuning. Making spacetime classical forces a trade-off between the diffusion it must exhibit and the decoherence it must inflict: lowering the noise to evade precision-gravity bounds raises the decoherence until interference experiments exclude it, and lowering the decoherence raises the noise. The theory's dimensionless couplings are therefore bounded above and below by unrelated experiments — one coupling in the renormalisation paper's treatment, two once the sectors are resolved. A confirmed observation of gravitationally induced entanglement would close the question outright.

## The squeeze

$$
\underbrace{\text{precision gravimetry}}_{\text{upper bound on noise}}
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
\underbrace{\text{interference experiments}}_{\text{lower bound on coherence time}} .
$$

The sources quote the surviving window three times, and the three are not commensurable. They must not be chained.

| Source | Quantity | Window |
|---|---|---|
| Rotation-curve paper (2024) | dimensionful $D_0c^3$ | $10^{-2}$ to $10^{24}\ \mathrm{m^3kg^{-2}s^{-1}}$, about 26 orders |
| Renormalisation paper | dimensionless $D_G$, a single coupling | $10^{-63}$ to $10^{-54}$, about 9 orders |
| Stochastic-modes paper (2026, newest) | dimensionless $D_2$, now resolved by sector | $10^{-71}$ to $10^{-66}$, about 5 orders |

Two cautions belong with that table, and they matter more than the headline number.

**The last two rows concern the same symbol and do not overlap.** $D_G$ and $D_2$ name the same dimensionless diffusion coupling; the phantom-dark-matter paper relabels the renormalisation paper's $D_G\leq10^{-54}$ as $D_2\lesssim10^{-54}$. Yet the newest window tops out at $10^{-66}$. The two ranges are disjoint, and the module records that as an unresolved discrepancy across the sources rather than reconciling it.

**The 5-order window is not a window on one coupling.** Its upper end is a *tensor-sector* bound from LIGO stochastic-gravitational-wave data, which the same paper says lies about ten orders below the *scalar* bound it obtains from LISA Pathfinder noise; its lower end is a generic molecular-coherence bound. The newest treatment in fact has **two** dimensionless couplings, with the noise bound fixing one combination and the gravitational-wave bound another, so the tight figure pairs constraints on different objects.

The individual bounds behind the first row are the Hoyle *et al.* torsion pendulum and the Westphal *et al.* millimetre-mass experiment from below, and fullerene interferometry — via the decoherence rate it would imply — from above. The verdict in the sources is that the theory "is currently viable, with the proviso that the IR regularisation needs to be better understood."

## Which experiment counts, and where

The papers do not agree on how to use LISA Pathfinder, and the disagreement should be recorded rather than smoothed. The rotation-curve paper **excludes** differential-acceleration measurements — LISA Pathfinder among them, by citation rather than by name — on the grounds that low-frequency fluctuations may affect both masses or paths alike, adding that the matter "requires some further understanding of on-shell versus off-shell contributions." The renormalisation and stochastic-modes papers do use LISA Pathfinder's excess noise to bound the coupling. Anyone citing a Pathfinder bound should say which treatment they are following.

The prospective improvement belongs to LISA itself, not to Pathfinder: the estimate is that the lower bound rises by at least ten orders of magnitude once LISA is operational.

## Sector-resolved bounds

The scalar-vector-tensor decomposition of [[stochastic-modes]] separates what each experiment sees. Fluctuations of the Newtonian potential $\Phi$ are what the excess-noise bound constrains, fixing one combination of the theory's two dimensionless couplings; bounds on the stochastic gravitational-wave energy density in an FLRW background constrain another. Decoherence rates depend on fluctuations in both $\Phi$ and the curvature perturbation $\psi$. Before that decomposition all of these were folded into a single coefficient.

The distinctive signature is the shape of the acceleration power spectral density. Lorentz invariance severely restricts its form, so the variance in acceleration depends on frequency and on the radius of the test mass but not on its mass — which the source notes is typical of many noise processes rather than unusual.

That same paper records a near-exclusion. If the computed spectrum is assumed to hold at all scales, the bound demands an ultraviolet cutoff far above the millimetre scale to which gravity has been tested, and with scale-independent couplings the theory would be ruled out. The escape is the running of the coupling, which is itself not computed.

## The decisive test

Because *local* CQ dynamics cannot generate entanglement, gravitationally induced entanglement experiments of the Bose--Marletto--Vedral type are falsifying rather than merely constraining. A confirmed observation would rule out this theory and every local classical-quantum theory of its kind. The locality hypothesis is not decoration: nonlocal noise kernels, including those implementing Diósi--Penrose decoherence, can generate entanglement and are not excluded by this argument.

## What weakens the bounds

Relating tabletop scales to astrophysical or cosmological ones requires the renormalisation-group flow of the couplings and whether the fluctuations acquire a mass. Neither is understood; the phantom-dark-matter paper says the mapping cannot currently be performed reliably, and the cosmological papers proceed by assuming laboratory bounds apply unchanged.

The cosmological claims in [[cosmological-claims]] add free parameters — an undetermined time scale in the rotation-curve work, an infrared cut-off scaling in the phantom-dark-matter work — which are fixed by the consistency they are meant to establish.

And the phantom-dark-matter paper, quoting the renormalisation paper's LISA Pathfinder bound $D_2\lesssim10^{-54}$, adds that it holds "in the case the fluctuations have no effective mass." The renormalisation paper's own version of the caveat is that a mass induced by coupling to matter would modify the two-point function. Whether the fluctuations have one is open.
